AsWGy698Wgo.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 28: Eighth Night of Tahajjud
AsWGy698Wgo.one_line: On the last Friday of Ramadan: the hadith of Jibril's mirror, Friday as the Day of Increase in Paradise, and ihsan as the path to seeing Allah.
AsWGy698Wgo.summary: The twenty-eighth night falls on the last Friday of Ramadan, and the reminder between the rakaat explains why Friday matters so much. The speaker narrates the hadith recorded by al-Tabarani in which Jibril brings the Prophet a mirror with a black spot in it: the mirror is Friday, given to this ummah, and the spot is the Hour, which will be established on a Friday. In Paradise the same day is called the Day of Increase. Its people are gathered, pulpits of light are set up for the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs, and then their Lord reveals Himself and they look upon Him, a gift beyond anything an eye has seen, an ear has heard or a heart has imagined. He ties this to the verse that promises those who do good the best reward and more, which the exegetes explain as Paradise and then the sight of Allah's face. The road to that increase is ihsan: worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and knowing that even if you do not see Him, He sees you. He closes by asking Allah to make the congregation people of ihsan, to grant them the sight of Him in the Hereafter, and to accept their repentance.

outline.gist: This night is the last Friday of the blessed month, so he sets out to explain from a hadith why Friday is so important, especially for believers who rise at night to pray together.

outline.gist: On that day in Paradise pulpits of light are set up for the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs, then their Lord reveals Himself to them and they look upon Him and are invited to ask.

outline.heading: What no eye has seen and no heart has imagined
outline.gist: What Allah gives on that day surpasses anything an eye has seen, an ear has heard or a human heart has imagined.

outline.heading: The best reward and more: Paradise and the sight of Allah
outline.gist: Jibril calls it the Day of Increase, matching the verse that those who do good receive the best reward and more; the exegetes say the best reward is Paradise and the increase is seeing Allah's face.

outline.heading: Ihsan: worship as though you see Him
outline.gist: The increase is promised to people of ihsan, who worship Allah as though they see Him, knowing He sees them; he asks Allah to make the congregation among them, to grant them the sight of Him and to accept their repentance.

sOKBeb92x-g.speaker_note: Tazkiyah Pearls series by the sheikh; single voice referring to the series' earlier sessions
sOKBeb92x-g.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 19: Love
sOKBeb92x-g.one_line: Love as the soul of tazkiyah: a commitment before an emotion, reached through loving the Prophet, and the only lasting motive for faith.
sOKBeb92x-g.summary: He calls love the spirit of the whole tazkiyah journey and of Islam itself: Allah loved us into existence and our purpose is to love Him back. Since love is hard to define, he first clears away fish love, loving what someone does for you, and love produced by a fluctuating self-value, both of which fade. Real love begins as a commitment to treat someone as an extension of yourself; the emotion comes later, as the heart slowly mixes what it is exposed to. Fear and hope are useful short-term motives, but only love can sustain decades of faith, and its true opposite is indifference. Because loving an unseen God is hard, the door is loving the Prophet, whom you can only love by knowing him, and he dares anyone to study him and not love him. He walks through the hadith of the three things that bring the sweetness of faith, Umar's admission that he loved the Prophet less than himself and his change, and his triangle of love, compassion and humility, without which love turns possessive or cruel. He ends with the Prophet's dua for Allah's love and Heraclius's observation that no one leaves this faith once it enters the heart, urging listeners to commit and let the feeling grow.

outline.heading: Opening
Love as the spirit and soul of tazkiyah
outline.gist: Left for last because it ties everything together; hard to attain, but once obtained it fixes problems at their source.

outline.heading: Islam is rooted in Allah's love for us
outline.gist: Allah showed us love by giving us life, and our purpose is to love Him back; yet scholars struggle to define love.

outline.heading: Humans crave love
outline.gist: A loveless life feels empty; people full of love come to Islam through intellectual questions rather than inner emptiness.

outline.heading: Love differs by its object; stories of the pious
outline.gist: Love for parents, children, spouse and friends differ yet share a thread; reading stories of those who loved Allah helps generate it.

outline.heading: Fish love: loving what someone does for you
outline.gist: We say we love fish and then pull it from the water and eat it; much human love is love of what others give us.

outline.heading: Love born of fluctuating self-value is toxic
outline.gist: Loving someone because they make you feel more about yourself fades as soon as they stop.

outline.heading: Love is a commitment: the other as an extension of you
outline.gist: Their pain is your pain and their gain your gain; a love that never supports or helps is meaningless, and love paired with abuse is harmful.

outline.heading: A father's love proven by deeds
outline.gist: He may never have said it, but a father who always put his child first showed his love through action.

outline.heading: The emotion comes slowly, especially for Allah
outline.gist: The heart needs long exposure and positive thought to produce love; loving an unseen, unheard divine being has no precedent in our experience.

outline.heading: Fear and hope are short-term; love lasts
outline.gist: Fear and reward are quick fixes against laziness or deviation, but only love can keep someone committed for sixty years.

outline.heading: The opposite of love is indifference
outline.gist: Hate is love inverted; fluctuating religious commitment comes from a lack of love, which is an infinite fuel.

outline.heading: Loving the Prophet is the door to loving Allah
outline.gist: Everything we know about Allah came through the Prophet, and his example shows what loving Allah looks like.

outline.heading: The sweetness of faith: you enjoy what you love
outline.gist: The hadith of three things that bring the sweetness of iman; at the peak of training the nafs, it falls in love and worship becomes easy.

outline.heading: Give us rest through it, Bilal
outline.gist: The Prophet found his rest in prayer, the opposite of rushing through it, because he loved it.

outline.heading: First: Allah and His Prophet most beloved
outline.gist: The companions loved the Prophet and he taught them to love Allah; you cannot love someone you do not know, so study him, and he dares anyone to do so and not love him.

outline.heading: Second: loving others only for Allah's sake
outline.gist: Wanting nothing from someone, not admiration, loyalty or wealth, only that they reach Paradise and that you get there together.

outline.heading: Third: hating to leave Islam like being thrown into fire
outline.gist: Loving Allah, His Prophet, Islam and the Muslims brings joy in saying Allah's name and in all worship.

outline.heading: Umar: loving the Prophet more than himself
outline.gist: Umar admitted he loved the Prophet more than all but himself, then returned to say he now loved him more; he explained it to his son by remembering that the Prophet led him from Hellfire to Paradise.

outline.heading: The triangle of love, compassion and humility
outline.gist: Without humility love becomes possessive and narcissistic; without compassion it flips to hatred, as in bitter divorces.

outline.heading: Commit first and the heart follows
outline.gist: With humility and compassion as a baseline, committing to what you should love lets the heart generate the emotion that fuels you for life.

outline.heading: Lives explainable only by love
outline.gist: The Prophet's nightly hours of recitation and scholars he met who were fulfilled by remembering Allah show that love, not force, sustains worship.

outline.heading: The Prophet's dua for Allah's love
outline.gist: He asked for Allah's love, the love of those who love Him, and deeds that bring Him closer; what he was given or denied would be used for what Allah loves.

outline.heading: Love is attainable with the right pieces
outline.gist: Stable self-value, humility, compassion, putting others and Allah's commands first, and learning about the Prophet will eventually produce the feeling.

outline.heading: Heraclius and Abu Sufyan: no one leaves
outline.gist: Forced to be truthful, Abu Sufyan admitted the Prophet's followers kept growing and none left; once faith's joy enters the heart it is never given up.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Love: of Allah, the Prophet, and one another
themes.note: Love as commitment before emotion, the only lasting motive in faith, reached through loving the Prophet.

themes.label: Self-value, self-worth, confidence
themes.note: Love that depends on someone making you feel better about yourself is toxic and fades.

themes.label: Hope, fear and the balance between them
themes.note: Fear and hope of reward work as quick fixes, but not as the long-term engine of faith.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: Knowing the Prophet leads to loving him, and he teaches how to love Allah.

themes.label: Eman: faith, certainty, doubt
themes.note: The hadith of the three things that bring the sweetness of faith.

themes.label: Brotherhood, companionship and friendship
themes.note: Loving others for Allah's sake means wanting only their success in the hereafter.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Humility and compassion are prerequisites without which love turns possessive or cruel.

hadith.gist: Three things, whoever has them finds the sweetness of faith: Allah and His Messenger being dearer than all else, loving a person only for Allah, and hating to return to disbelief as one hates being thrown into fire.
The Prophet would tell Bilal to call the prayer so they could find rest in it.
None of you truly believes until I am dearer to him than himself, his family, children, wealth and all people; Umar's exchange with the Prophet about loving him more than himself.
Dua: O Allah, I ask You for Your love, the love of those who love You, and the love of deeds that bring me closer to Your love.
Heraclius questioned Abu Sufyan about the Prophet's followers and concluded that faith, once its joy enters the heart, is never abandoned.

maxims: Fish love
Love is a commitment before it is an emotion
The opposite of love is indifference
Love the Prophet and he will take you to Allah
I dare you to know him and not love him
Love, compassion and humbleness: the triangle

stories.who: Heraclius and Abu Sufyan

takeaways: Treat love as a commitment: support, help and sacrifice for those you say you love
Study the Prophet's life and character until he becomes the most beloved to you
Love others only for Allah's sake, wanting nothing but their success in the hereafter
Build humility and compassion as the baseline for any genuine love
Make the Prophet's dua for Allah's love part of your routine

60:10.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا جَآءَكُمُ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتُ مُهَٰجِرَٰتࣲ فَٱمۡتَحِنُوهُنَّۖ ٱللَّهُ أَعۡلَمُ بِإِيمَٰنِهِنَّۖ فَإِنۡ عَلِمۡتُمُوهُنَّ مُؤۡمِنَٰتࣲ فَلَا تَرۡجِعُوهُنَّ إِلَى ٱلۡكُفَّارِۖ لَا هُنَّ حِلࣱّ لَّهُمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يَحِلُّونَ لَهُنَّۖ وَءَاتُوهُم مَّآ أَنفَقُواْۚ وَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ أَن تَنكِحُوهُنَّ إِذَآ ءَاتَيۡتُمُوهُنَّ أُجُورَهُنَّۚ وَلَا تُمۡسِكُواْ بِعِصَمِ ٱلۡكَوَافِرِ وَسۡـَٔلُواْ مَآ أَنفَقۡتُمۡ وَلۡيَسۡـَٔلُواْ مَآ أَنفَقُواْۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ حُكۡمُ ٱللَّهِ يَحۡكُمُ بَيۡنَكُمۡۖ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمࣱ‏
60:10.en: O ye who believe! When believing women come unto you as fugitives, examine them. Allah is Best Aware of their faith. Then, if ye know them for true believers, send them not back unto the disbelievers. They are not lawful for them (the disbelievers), nor are they (the disbelievers) lawful for them. And give them (the disbelievers) that which they have spent (upon them). And it is no sin for you to marry such women when ye have given them their dues. And hold not to the ties of disbelieving women; and ask for (the return of) that which ye have spent; and let them (the disbelievers) ask for that which they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah. He judgeth between you. Allah is Knower, Wise

60:11.ar: وَإِن فَاتَكُمۡ شَيۡءࣱ مِّنۡ أَزۡوَٰجِكُمۡ إِلَى ٱلۡكُفَّارِ فَعَاقَبۡتُمۡ فَـَٔاتُواْ ٱلَّذِينَ ذَهَبَتۡ أَزۡوَٰجُهُم مِّثۡلَ مَآ أَنفَقُواْۚ وَٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ ٱلَّذِيٓ أَنتُم بِهِۦ مُؤۡمِنُونَ
60:11.en: And if any of your wives have gone from you unto the disbelievers and afterward ye have your turn (of triumph), then give unto those whose wives have gone the like of that which they have spent, and keep your duty to Allah in Whom ye are believers

60:12.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِيُّ إِذَا جَآءَكَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتُ يُبَايِعۡنَكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن لَّا يُشۡرِكۡنَ بِٱللَّهِ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَا يَسۡرِقۡنَ وَلَا يَزۡنِينَ وَلَا يَقۡتُلۡنَ أَوۡلَٰدَهُنَّ وَلَا يَأۡتِينَ بِبُهۡتَٰنࣲ يَفۡتَرِينَهُۥ بَيۡنَ أَيۡدِيهِنَّ وَأَرۡجُلِهِنَّ وَلَا يَعۡصِينَكَ فِي مَعۡرُوفࣲ فَبَايِعۡهُنَّ وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡ لَهُنَّ ٱللَّهَۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
60:12.en: O Prophet! If believing women come unto thee, taking oath of allegiance unto thee that they will ascribe no thing as partner unto Allah, and will neither steal nor commit adultery nor kill their children, nor produce any lie that they have devised between their hands and feet, nor disobey thee in what is right, then accept their allegiance and ask Allah to forgive them. Lo! Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

66:1.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِيُّ لِمَ تُحَرِّمُ مَآ أَحَلَّ ٱللَّهُ لَكَۖ تَبۡتَغِي مَرۡضَاتَ أَزۡوَٰجِكَۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
66:1.en: O Prophet! Why bannest thou that which Allah hath made lawful for thee, seeking to please thy wives? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

66:2.ar: قَدۡ فَرَضَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡ تَحِلَّةَ أَيۡمَٰنِكُمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ مَوۡلَىٰكُمۡۖ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
66:2.en: Allah hath made lawful for you (Muslims) absolution from your oaths (of such a kind), and Allah is your Protector. He is the Knower, the Wise

66:3.ar: وَإِذۡ أَسَرَّ ٱلنَّبِيُّ إِلَىٰ بَعۡضِ أَزۡوَٰجِهِۦ حَدِيثࣰ ا فَلَمَّا نَبَّأَتۡ بِهِۦ وَأَظۡهَرَهُ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡهِ عَرَّفَ بَعۡضَهُۥ وَأَعۡرَضَ عَنۢ بَعۡضࣲۖ فَلَمَّا نَبَّأَهَا بِهِۦ قَالَتۡ مَنۡ أَنۢبَأَكَ هَٰذَاۖ قَالَ نَبَّأَنِيَ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ ٱلۡخَبِيرُ
66:3.en: When the Prophet confided a fact unto one of his wives and when she afterward divulged it and Allah apprised him thereof, he made known (to her) part thereof and passed over part. And when he told it her she said: Who hath told thee? He said: The Knower, the Aware hath told me

66:4.ar: إِن تَتُوبَآ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ فَقَدۡ صَغَتۡ قُلُوبُكُمَاۖ وَإِن تَظَٰهَرَا عَلَيۡهِ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ مَوۡلَىٰهُ وَجِبۡرِيلُ وَصَٰلِحُ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَۖ وَٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ بَعۡدَ ذَٰلِكَ ظَهِيرٌ
66:4.en: If ye twain turn unto Allah repentant, (ye have cause to do so) for your hearts desired (the ban); and if ye aid one another against him (Muhammad) then lo! Allah, even He, is his Protecting Friend, and Gabriel and the righteous among the believers; and furthermore the angels are his helpers

68:51.ar: وَإِن يَكَادُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ لَيُزۡلِقُونَكَ بِأَبۡصَٰرِهِمۡ لَمَّا سَمِعُواْ ٱلذِّكۡرَ وَيَقُولُونَ إِنَّهُۥ لَمَجۡنُونࣱ‏
68:51.en: And lo! those who disbelieve would fain disconcert thee with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say: Lo! he is indeed mad

68:4.en: And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature

Zs1V5997pHA.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 27: A Code of Conduct
Zs1V5997pHA.one_line: Religiosity without ethics fails: the women's pledge, the Prophet's restraint with his wives, and enemies who searched his life for a flaw.
Zs1V5997pHA.summary: On the twenty-seventh night he warns that religiosity cut off from ethics becomes an empty shell that repels people. The traveller whose dua is not answered because his food and clothing are haram shows that sincerity and humility cannot cover bad conduct, and Laylat al-Qadr's date was lifted because two men quarreled, so hearts must be cleared of hatred and wrongs repaired before these nights. From Al-Mumtahanah 60:12 he walks through the pledge taken from women who fled to Medina, the same pledge as the first Aqabah: no shirk, theft, adultery, harming children, slander, or refusing a good instruction. Obedience to anyone is limited to what is good and ethical; following unethical orders, whether as a soldier or under a medical supervisor, brings equal accountability. From At-Tahrim 66:3 he shows the Prophet correcting only the broken confidence that mattered for the relationship and passing over the conspiracy, refusing the petty satisfaction of proving himself right, a lesson in maturity before marriage and friendship. From Al-Qalam 68:51 he notes that Quraysh searched his whole life for an ethical slip and could only call him mad. He asks listeners to come to Allah with their conduct repaired and to ask His help where they fall short.

outline.heading: The cultural pull of the 27th night
outline.gist: He does not oppose the attachment to the 27th night, only treating it as the one night worth effort; some companions held firmly that it is the night.

outline.heading: The Quran's code of conduct
outline.gist: The Quran sets a standard of ethics we will be held to, often shown through the higher standard the Prophet was held to.

outline.heading: Religiosity without ethicality
outline.gist: When focus on reward, punishment and ritual is detached from moral standards, ideologies decay into a shell of rituals.

outline.heading: Ritual zeal with bad conduct repels people
outline.gist: People fussing over ritual details while eating haram, abusing family or lying in business drive others away from religion, and Muslims are not exempt.

outline.heading: Seeking this night's mercy requires ethics
outline.gist: Asking for forgiveness and freedom from punishment means coming to Allah with some degree of morality, not only rituals.

outline.heading: The traveller whose dua is not answered
outline.gist: He has every outer and inner sign of acceptance, yet his food, drink and clothing are haram, so how could he be answered?

outline.heading: Fear coming to Allah with bad conduct
outline.gist: Rudeness, arrogance, abuse and taking what is not yours can cancel sincere worship and its blessing.

outline.heading: Slamming shut the doors Allah opens
outline.gist: Oppressing a spouse, mistreating children or employees, lying in business or cheating on exams can make all the nights of worship add up to nothing.

outline.heading: The night forgotten because two men quarreled
outline.gist: The Prophet was told the date of Laylat al-Qadr but forgot it while stopping two fasting men shouting obscenities, a lesson that disputes cost us blessing.

outline.heading: Cleanse your heart of hatred and repair wrongs
outline.gist: On blessed nights Allah forgives all except the one who associates partners and the one who harbours hatred; reach out and apologize to anyone you wronged.

outline.heading: Believing women who fled to Medina
outline.gist: The Prophet refused to return women escaping oppression despite the treaty, but was told to test their sincerity in case they were spies.

outline.heading: Their pledge matches the first pledge of Aqabah
outline.gist: The first Aqabah pledge, taken from twelve men of Yathrib, was ethical, unlike the commitment-driven second pledge, and the women's pledge used the same words.

outline.heading: First element: no shirk, the cornerstone
outline.gist: Tawhid is the foundation that protects the deen and everything else ranks after it.

outline.heading: Second element: no theft
outline.gist: They pledged not to steal.

outline.heading: Third element: no adultery
outline.gist: They pledged not to commit zina.

outline.heading: Fourth element: no harming children
outline.gist: Not only killing but any spiritual or financial harm or abandonment of children.

outline.heading: Fifth element: no slander or false testimony
outline.gist: No invented lies, false witness or spreading rumours.

outline.heading: Sixth element: obey only in what is good
outline.gist: Obedience is owed only to beneficial, ethical commands, whether from a spouse, an imam or a ruler.

outline.heading: No excuse of following orders
outline.gist: If a superior orders you to break the law or harm someone, you refuse and bear the consequences; 'I was just a soldier' is no defence.

outline.heading: Unethical orders in medicine
outline.gist: Trainees are taught to refuse unethical instructions even from a supervisor who controls their career, because they are equally accountable.

outline.heading: The code of conduct Muslims must represent
outline.gist: All six elements are ethical; this pledge was required before the move to Medina, and ethics must be solid before religiosity benefits anyone.

outline.heading: The honey incident
outline.gist: Two wives, jealous of his visits to another wife who served honey, told the Prophet he had bad breath, so he vowed never to eat it again and asked that it stay private.

outline.heading: A confidence broken
outline.gist: The wife he confided in spread the secret, hurting the wife who offered the honey; Jibril told him everything, including the conspiracy.

outline.heading: He mentioned part and passed over part
outline.gist: He did not accuse them of conspiring; he only addressed the broken confidence, because a relationship cannot survive without trust.

outline.heading: They learned he knew only from the recitation
outline.gist: The wives realized he had known of the conspiracy when they heard the verses recited in prayer, yet he had said nothing.

outline.heading: The petty high of 'I told you so'
outline.gist: He jokes about keeping notes for years to prove himself right; the feeling is fulfilling but petty and helps no one, and the Prophet took no pleasure in it.

outline.heading: Correct for their benefit, not yours
outline.gist: Exposing the conspiracy would only soothe him; the lesson they needed was keeping confidences, since he would keep entrusting them with secrets.

outline.heading: An invitation to repent, never raised again
outline.gist: The verses invite them to tawbah and declare Allah, Jibril, the believers and the angels his supporters; he never held it against them.

outline.heading: Maturity before marriage
outline.gist: A need to always be right leaves a person lonely and unloved; in relationships rarely does anyone care who was right, except on matters like trust.

outline.heading: Let it go or end up friendless
outline.gist: Pointing out every mistake a friend makes slowly drives friends away.

outline.heading: Never forbid yourself what Allah made lawful
outline.gist: The Prophet was also corrected: making something haram on yourself to please someone breeds resentment.

outline.heading: Four needs for representing Islam
outline.gist: The surahs at the start of the twenty-ninth juz supply knowledge, ethics, emotional investment and action; Al-Qalam covers ethics.

outline.heading: Quraysh frustrated by a compelling message
outline.gist: Al-Qalam opens by praising his character; the message was so compelling that Quraysh kept losing people's loyalty.

outline.heading: Interlude
Searching for dirt and finding none
outline.gist: They investigated his friends, partners, employees, relatives and wives for something to use against him and found nothing.

outline.heading: Staring to make him slip
outline.gist: The rare word for slipping refers to a moral lapse, not a physical fall; they glared at him hoping for any ethical mistake.

outline.heading: Madness is not an ethical charge
outline.gist: All they could say was that he was mad, which accuses nothing about his character, unlike lying, theft or adultery.

outline.heading: How much would they find on you?
outline.gist: If someone paid investigators to dig into our lives they would find plenty; we ask Allah to conceal us.

outline.heading: Bring your conduct with your dua
outline.gist: When raising your hands tonight, observe the code of ethics, confess where you have wronged people, and ask Allah to make you better.

outline.heading: Outro

3:113.ar: ۞لَيۡسُواْ سَوَآءࣰۗ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ أُمَّةࣱ قَآئِمَةࣱ يَتۡلُونَ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ ءَانَآءَ ٱلَّيۡلِ وَهُمۡ يَسۡجُدُونَ
3:113.en: They are not all alike. Of the People of the Scripture there is a staunch community who recite the revelations of Allah in the night season, falling prostrate (before Him)

3:75.ar: ۞وَمِنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ مَنۡ إِن تَأۡمَنۡهُ بِقِنطَارࣲ يُؤَدِّهِۦٓ إِلَيۡكَ وَمِنۡهُم مَّنۡ إِن تَأۡمَنۡهُ بِدِينَارࣲ لَّا يُؤَدِّهِۦٓ إِلَيۡكَ إِلَّا مَا دُمۡتَ عَلَيۡهِ قَآئِمࣰ اۗ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمۡ قَالُواْ لَيۡسَ عَلَيۡنَا فِي ٱلۡأُمِّيِّـۧنَ سَبِيلࣱ وَيَقُولُونَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلۡكَذِبَ وَهُمۡ يَعۡلَمُونَ
3:75.en: Among the People of the Scripture there is he who, if thou trust him with a weight of treasure, will return it to thee. And among them there is he who, if thou trust him with a piece of gold, will not return it to thee unless thou keep standing over him. That is because they say: We have no duty to the Gentiles. They speak a lie concerning Allah knowingly

43:81.ar: قُلۡ إِن كَانَ لِلرَّحۡمَٰنِ وَلَدࣱ فَأَنَا۠ أَوَّلُ ٱلۡعَٰبِدِينَ
43:81.en: Say (O Muhammad): If the Beneficent One hath a son, then, I shall be first among the worshippers. (But there is no son)

34:24.ar: ۞قُلۡ مَن يَرۡزُقُكُم مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ قُلِ ٱللَّهُۖ وَإِنَّآ أَوۡ إِيَّاكُمۡ لَعَلَىٰ هُدًى أَوۡ فِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
34:24.en: Say: Who giveth you provision from the sky and the earth? Say: Allah, Lo! we or you assuredly are rightly guided or in error manifest

60:7.ar: ۞عَسَى ٱللَّهُ أَن يَجۡعَلَ بَيۡنَكُمۡ وَبَيۡنَ ٱلَّذِينَ عَادَيۡتُم مِّنۡهُم مَّوَدَّةࣰۚ وَٱللَّهُ قَدِيرࣱۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
60:7.en: It may be that Allah will ordain love between you and those of them with whom ye are at enmity. Allah is Mighty, and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

60:8.ar: لَّا يَنۡهَىٰكُمُ ٱللَّهُ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ لَمۡ يُقَٰتِلُوكُمۡ فِي ٱلدِّينِ وَلَمۡ يُخۡرِجُوكُم مِّن دِيَٰرِكُمۡ أَن تَبَرُّوهُمۡ وَتُقۡسِطُوٓاْ إِلَيۡهِمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلۡمُقۡسِطِينَ
60:8.en: Allah forbiddeth you not those who warred not against you on account of religion and drove you not out from your homes, that ye should show them kindness and deal justly with them. Lo! Allah loveth the just dealers

60:9.ar: إِنَّمَا يَنۡهَىٰكُمُ ٱللَّهُ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ قَٰتَلُوكُمۡ فِي ٱلدِّينِ وَأَخۡرَجُوكُم مِّن دِيَٰرِكُمۡ وَظَٰهَرُواْ عَلَىٰٓ إِخۡرَاجِكُمۡ أَن تَوَلَّوۡهُمۡۚ وَمَن يَتَوَلَّهُمۡ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ
60:9.en: Allah forbiddeth you only those who warred against you on account of religion and have driven you out from your homes and helped to drive you out, that ye make friends of them. Whosoever maketh friends of them - (All) such are wrong-doers

9:4.ar: إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ عَٰهَدتُّم مِّنَ ٱلۡمُشۡرِكِينَ ثُمَّ لَمۡ يَنقُصُوكُمۡ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَمۡ يُظَٰهِرُواْ عَلَيۡكُمۡ أَحَدࣰ ا فَأَتِمُّوٓاْ إِلَيۡهِمۡ عَهۡدَهُمۡ إِلَىٰ مُدَّتِهِمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلۡمُتَّقِينَ
9:4.en: Excepting those of the idolaters with whom ye (Muslims) have a treaty, and who have since abated nothing of your right nor have supported anyone against you. (As for these), fulfil their treaty to them till their term. Lo! Allah loveth those who keep their duty (unto Him)

30:3.ar: فِيٓ أَدۡنَى ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَهُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ غَلَبِهِمۡ سَيَغۡلِبُونَ
30:3.en: In the nearer land, and they, after their defeat will be victorious

30:4.ar: فِي بِضۡعِ سِنِينَۗ لِلَّهِ ٱلۡأَمۡرُ مِن قَبۡلُ وَمِنۢ بَعۡدُۚ وَيَوۡمَئِذࣲ يَفۡرَحُ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ
30:4.en: Within ten years - Allah's is the command in the former case and in the latter - and in that day believers will rejoice

30:5.ar: بِنَصۡرِ ٱللَّهِۚ يَنصُرُ مَن يَشَآءُۖ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
30:5.en: In Allah's help to victory. He helpeth to victory whom He will. He is the Mighty, the Merciful

MPICyzvMxoM.speaker_note: sixth episode of his Pointing Out the Obvious series; refers to his annual course and arriving from Syria in 2013
MPICyzvMxoM.title: Pointing Out the Obvious 6: Tolerance
MPICyzvMxoM.one_line: How Muslims should relate to people of other faiths: see the good in them, befriend and collaborate, ally only against oppression, and leave destinations to Allah.
MPICyzvMxoM.summary: Responding to frequent questions from young people, the sheikh argues that relations with people of other faiths were never confusing to the Companions. Goodness exists in everyone, and the Quran repeatedly stops Muslims from demonising whole groups. Muslims may befriend non-Muslims and are obliged to collaborate with other faith communities as a form of dawah, fearing no debate because their arguments are strong. He explains that the verses translated as forbidding friendship refer to political alliance, citing Surat al-Mumtahanah: kindness and fairness toward all who do not fight Muslims or expel them, and no alliance with oppressors. He contrasts Muslim restraint with the media amplification of Muslim extremists, which he ties to political distraction and to his frustration at ISIS questions while the Syrian regime committed far worse. Prophetic examples follow: the Constitution of Medina, the alliance with Khuza'a, repeatedly renewed treaties, the context of Surat al-Tawbah, the Muslims' joy at the Roman victory, protected minorities and the Jews who left Andalusia with the Muslims, and Ali working for a Jewish orchard owner. He ends by forbidding speculation on where others will end up: the Quran gives warnings and glad tidings, not a catalogue of destinations, so worry about your own.

outline.heading: Why tolerance should not be confusing
outline.gist: Young people ask about this often, yet the Companions only questioned genuine wartime dilemmas, such as facing a father in battle or visiting a pagan mother.

outline.heading: There is good in everyone
outline.gist: Good is done by people of every faith; believing it comes only through Muslims is pathological.

outline.heading: The Quran: they are not all alike
outline.gist: Allah distinguishes the sincere and trustworthy among the People of the Book from those who cheat, because wartime pressure tempted Muslims to demonise everyone.

outline.heading: People are like metals
outline.gist: The Prophet said the best before Islam are the best in Islam, and he admired good qualities in pre-Islamic figures.

outline.heading: Seeing the good in the West and building on it
outline.gist: Muslims are quick to list Western faults while ignoring their own; ma'ruf means recognising existing good and strengthening it.

outline.heading: Friendship with non-Muslims
outline.gist: It is allowed and loving those who do no harm is required; what matters is a friend's values, while choosing your close circle carefully.

outline.heading: Interfaith collaboration is obligatory dawah
outline.gist: Visiting churches and synagogues and hosting them is how people learn Islam; we have nothing to hide and no fear of losing our faith.

outline.heading: Which debates to accept
outline.gist: Refuse debates that only give nonsense a platform, like whether voting is allowed, but engage meaningful ones confidently, as the Quran invites opponents to bring proof.

outline.heading: We do not judge where others are going
outline.gist: Muslims have long led interfaith debate; they deliver the Quran's warnings and glad tidings and leave destinations to Allah.

outline.heading: Befriending means political alliance
outline.gist: Translations that say do not befriend them mislead readers; the verses forbid alliances with enemies at war who deny your rights.

outline.heading: Al-Mumtahanah 7: love between you and your enemies
outline.gist: A late verse hopes Allah will turn enmity into mawaddah, the highest kind of love, and forgive past transgression; he knows no other scripture with such a verse.

outline.heading: Extremism is not more common among Muslims
outline.gist: Demonising peaceful fellow citizens reflects politically driven teaching; other faiths have more extremists but give them no airtime.

outline.heading: Why the world needs an enemy
outline.gist: Imperial powers use fear of outsiders, like sports, as a distraction so people do not question their own leaders.

outline.heading: Being asked about ISIS instead of the regime
outline.gist: Arriving from Syria, he was offended by ISIS questions when the regime had gassed villages and disappeared thousands.

outline.heading: Extremism in his own city is low
outline.gist: Among over forty thousand Muslims locally, extremist views are rarer than in many other communities.

outline.heading: Al-Mumtahanah 8: birr and fairness toward the peaceful
outline.gist: Allah encourages the kindness you show parents, plus fairness with compassion, toward those who neither fight your faith nor take your land and wealth.

outline.heading: Al-Mumtahanah 9: no alliance with oppressors
outline.gist: Only alliance, not emotion, is forbidden with those who fight your faith, expel you or help those who do; governments simply ignore these clear verses.

outline.heading: The Prophet with his non-Muslim neighbours
outline.gist: He visited, ate with and talked with Jewish neighbours and let dawah go when they were not interested.

outline.heading: Why he pressed Quraysh so hard
outline.gist: His persistence with the Qurayshi leaders was because they denied Muslims the right to speak, not to force guidance on them.

outline.heading: Alliances on shared concerns: sex education
outline.gist: Muslims should ally with Catholic school boards, churches and synagogues that share their concerns about what children are taught.

outline.heading: The Constitution of Medina
outline.gist: Every tribe and faith group signed it, named carefully one by one, and those who broke it by treachery were expelled.

outline.heading: The alliance with Khuza'a
outline.gist: Mostly non-Muslim allies were attacked while on pilgrimage, and the Prophet marched to defend them.

outline.heading: Treaties renewed through 27 betrayals
outline.gist: He kept renewing broken treaties until Surat al-Tawbah ended them, yet even then exempted tribes that never broke their word.

outline.heading: Surat al-Tawbah needs its context
outline.gist: The surah is full of justice once its circumstances are known; he plans an English tafsir of it.

outline.heading: Siding with the Romans against the Persians
outline.gist: The Quran validated the Muslims' sympathy for the Christian Romans and promised their victory within a few years.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr's bet on the Roman victory
outline.gist: Before betting was forbidden, he wagered six years; the victory came in the seventh.

outline.heading: Cheering for non-Muslim teams
outline.gist: Supporting any World Cup team is fine because sport is not war.

outline.heading: Protected minorities (ahl al-dhimmah)
outline.gist: Muslim states protected their worship, laws and contracts, and exempted them from military service in exchange for a tax.

outline.heading: Jews who left Andalusia with the Muslims
outline.gist: They chose to leave with the Muslims, and Jewish communities lived, traded and held office in Muslim cities for centuries; those who stayed were brutalised.

outline.heading: Ali works for a Jewish orchard owner
outline.gist: When the Prophet had nothing to eat, Ali irrigated a Jewish man's trees for dates without asking whether it was allowed, because it was obvious; he adds the playful story of the date pits.

outline.heading: Destinations: the Quran is not a catalogue
outline.gist: Asking where others are going is a recent, rude obsession; the Quran assigns outcomes to deeds, not verdicts to individuals.

outline.heading: The Prophet rebukes a claim about a fallen man
outline.gist: Companions declared a fallen fighter in Jannah and the Prophet corrected them, showing it is not our place to judge.

outline.heading: Syllogisms do not work for the unseen
outline.gist: Logic needs both premises in the observable world, and our knowledge of the unseen is very limited.

outline.heading: Interlude
Those never properly warned
outline.gist: The schools of theology agree that people who never received the message, or received it distorted, are not held accountable.

outline.heading: Muslim and non-Muslim in this life
outline.gist: This binary only sets legal and social terms such as marriage and says nothing about destination; being called kafir by a Christian is no insult.

outline.heading: Many categories on the Day of Judgment
outline.gist: Sinful believers, pre-Islamic monotheists, truth-seekers who never found it and the oppressed who never had a free choice all form different groups.

outline.heading: Worry about your own destination
outline.gist: Say honestly that you do not know; endings can change at the last moment, so fear for yourself rather than judge others.

outline.heading: Outro

PU2TD39EtlY.title: Pointing Out the Obvious 7: Cross-Gender Relationships
PU2TD39EtlY.one_line: Islam seeks regulated, clearly defined relationships between men and women, not full segregation; flirting, ill-defined friendships and blocked marriage are the real problems.
PU2TD39EtlY.summary: The sheikh argues that full segregation was never an Islamic goal; it comes from Bedouin and Victorian norms, while Islam aims at good manners, mutual respect and a regulated environment, with marriage made easy so people do not seek intimacy unlawfully. He sets out eight kinds of cross-gender relationship: emergency or medical, mahram, blood relatives, social acquaintances, professional, classmates, mentor and mentee, and spouses. Each is safe when clearly defined and kept within its lane, while vague labels like friends keep options open and invite trouble. He warns about power differentials, where vulnerability is mistaken for attraction, insisting that imams, teachers, physicians and employers carry the responsibility. The core problem is flirting: suggestive, ambiguous behaviour that seeks validation outside marriage, against which Islam values directness. He then describes the holistic social system: modest dress for both genders, lowered gaze, parameters on every relationship, families vetting suitors for compatibility, and caution with private texting as a virtual seclusion. Healthy jealousy and a spouse's feelings must be respected. He closes by asking young men to know whether they are truly ready for marriage and, if not, to be extra professional rather than keep a woman waiting.

outline.heading: Opening
Norms that used to be obvious
outline.gist: Gender norms have shifted beyond recognition in a century, yet for Muslims the basic rules are clear and not seriously disputed by scholars.

outline.heading: Full segregation is not Islamic: Bedouin law
outline.gist: Islam corrected strict Bedouin segregation, but later scholarship reacting to lost integrity regressed to it, while the Companions' lives show much more ordinary interaction.

outline.heading: Victorian norms and Islam's real aim
outline.gist: Aristocratic Victorian manners were also adopted wrongly; Islam aims at etiquette, mutual respect and a regulated environment.

outline.heading: Make the halal easy
outline.gist: Seeking intimacy is a human right; if communities make marriage hard and haram easy, people will flow to the lowest point.

outline.heading: Type 1: emergency and medical relationships
outline.gist: Saving a life or giving care lifts normal boundaries, yet physicians are bound by strict ethics such as chaperones.

outline.heading: Type 2: mahram relatives
outline.gist: Those you can never marry and have no desire for allow the most openness, unless circumstances such as siblings raised apart call for extra care.

outline.heading: Separate beds and the stepparent risk
outline.gist: The Prophet ordered children's beds separated; most abuse happens at home and risk rises with an unrelated man in the house, which past living arrangements avoided.

outline.heading: Turn to your mahram for emotional support
outline.gist: If you are not ready for marriage, invest in your mother, sisters and aunts rather than confiding in an attractive stranger.

outline.heading: Type 3: blood relatives and cousin marriage
outline.gist: Cousin marriage is normal worldwide and among the prophets; mocking it while normalising sex outside marriage shows lost moral bearings.

outline.heading: Well-defined relationships are safe
outline.gist: Clear definitions protect both people; the vague label friends keeps every option open, which is exactly why people like it.

outline.heading: Type 4: social acquaintances
outline.gist: Neighbours and family friends get greetings and talk within that frame; overlapping roles widen what can be discussed.

outline.heading: Type 5: professional relationships
outline.gist: Professionalism best describes most cross-gender dealings: kind and decent but directed at the shared work.

outline.heading: Type 6: classmates
outline.gist: The group that causes most problems; stay within the lane of learning together.

outline.heading: Type 7: mentor and mentee
outline.gist: Teaching and counselling are clearly defined, but well-defined relationships can still go wrong.

outline.heading: Power differentials and vulnerability
outline.gist: Someone who reveals their problems feels vulnerable, which the brain confuses with attraction; the stronger party must guard the line permanently.

outline.heading: Imams and the unmarried scholars
outline.gist: Imams who marry women who came for counselling exploit the role; unmarried early scholars wrote books rather than counselling women.

outline.heading: Employers and employees
outline.gist: A CEO also holds power over an employee's living and should treat the relationship like physician and patient.

outline.heading: Type 8: spouses
outline.gist: Marriage is the place for intimacy, flirting and the conversations that belong nowhere else.

outline.heading: Masjid norms in the Middle East
outline.gist: Women are confined to basements and an imam's involvement in a women's Quran programme would be scandalous there, a cultural norm he rejects.

outline.heading: The Prophet's masjid
outline.gist: Men in front and women behind with no barrier; men naturally waited until women left, without needing instruction.

outline.heading: Recap of the eight relationships
outline.gist: Every relationship must stay within its parameters.

outline.heading: The real problem: flirting
outline.gist: Flirting is suggestive, indirect behaviour that keeps the other guessing and opens the door for Shaytan; everyone knows when they are doing it.

outline.heading: Islam values directness
outline.gist: Openly stating marriage interest is fine; his test is whether you would be embarrassed if the conversation were recorded, which is also why dating's ambiguity is the problem.

outline.heading: Seeking validation outside marriage
outline.gist: Flirting is not haram in itself; it belongs with your spouse, and needing admiration from others signals a problem.

outline.heading: Serial flirts confuse communities
outline.gist: When several people ask him about the same person, that person is sending mixed messages, and enjoying being craved is a disease of the heart.

outline.heading: Come through the door, not the window
outline.gist: Flirting ends in either haram or marriage, so if marriage is the goal, propose properly and earn respect.

outline.heading: A holistic social system
outline.gist: Islam regulates gender relations as a whole society: everyone professional, boundaries respected, gaze lowered and modest dress; he also ties lapses to self-value and says some will need help to recover.

outline.heading: Dress code and male nature
outline.gist: Both genders cover, women with greater obligation and reward, because Islam acknowledges that men are more visually drawn.

outline.heading: Covering preserves marital attraction: his great-uncle's bedroom
outline.gist: Less public exposure keeps spouses attractive to each other; his elderly farmer relatives kept a lavishly cared-for bedroom, unlike many neglected ones today.

outline.heading: Covering demands respect for the mind
outline.gist: Hijab makes men attend to what a woman says, unlike interviews that ask actresses only about their diets.

outline.heading: Dress with an intention
outline.gist: Dressing to be respected versus dressing to be desired by everyone; nothing ever justifies harassment or rape.

outline.heading: Islam lowers outward temptation
outline.gist: Like zakat reducing theft, rulings make right choices easier, which is why young Muslims holding firm in the West are admirable.

outline.heading: Mixed friend groups
outline.gist: Undefined outings hide unspoken crushes and painful triangles; some separation in friend groups is healthier.

outline.heading: Delayed marriage is a systemic failure
outline.gist: Unmarried people into their thirties show that relationship parameters and the social system have broken down.

outline.heading: A father vets the suitor
outline.gist: Families protect lineage by testing a suitor's temper and character, once even by deliberately provoking him, to secure compatibility.

outline.heading: Let your parents help
outline.gist: A twenty-year-old has no experience of long-term relationships; arranged marriage is not Islamic, but parental input is wise.

outline.heading: The father's filter and broken homes
outline.gist: Fathers see whether a suitor is a man who will put her first; ignoring them often ends in divorce that children pay for.

outline.heading: Principle: defined relationships with etiquette are safe
outline.gist: His long working relationships with nurses and volunteers stay safe because purpose and manners are clear.

outline.heading: Principle: both genders lower the gaze
outline.gist: Men were addressed first in the Quran and are less likely to comply.

outline.heading: Principle: undefined friendship ends in disaster
outline.gist: Most television drama would vanish without ill-defined friendships between men and women.

outline.heading: Kindness is not flirting
outline.gist: Asking colleagues about their weekend or showing empathy is fine; the Prophet counselled women often and everyone felt safe with him.

outline.heading: Private texting is virtual seclusion
outline.gist: Most problems he sees start in private messages, where people say what they never would face to face.

outline.heading: Use group chats
outline.gist: Group messages keep communication transparent; if you cannot show someone your texts, you know they were wrong.

outline.heading: Blocking halal produces haram
outline.gist: Parents must judge suitors on compatibility, not personal or ethnic preferences, and ask what singles do for fifteen years without marriage.

outline.heading: Healthy jealousy
outline.gist: Some jealousy shows care; extreme jealousy needs professional help.

outline.heading: Respect your spouse's feelings
outline.gist: If a spouse is uneasy about a colleague, take it seriously; people read their own gender well.

outline.heading: Islam recognises human nature
outline.gist: Rulings vary by gender, setting and age, as with older women who no longer seek marriage.

outline.heading: Are you on the market?
outline.gist: Young men not ready for marriage should be extra professional rather than keep a woman waiting for years.

outline.heading: Outro

_7YhrqUrFIE.title: Ramadan Reminders 1446: The Last Hour of Ramadan
_7YhrqUrFIE.one_line: Last Jumuah of Ramadan 2025: push to the final hour, protect the gains afterwards, make Eid joyful, and vote for Gaza in the coming election.
_7YhrqUrFIE.summary: Delivered on the last Friday of Ramadan 1446, the khutbah argues that nothing is over while a moment remains. Just as a person with one breath left can still repent, a fast with one hour left can still be turned around, so he asks everyone to sit alone in the hour before Maghrib on the final day and make dua as the month slips away. His proof is the Prophet's tenth-year Hajj season: after Khadijah and Abu Talib died and twenty-six tribes refused him, he stayed in Mina until the grounds were empty and spoke to six poor young men who were still waiting to shave their heads. They became the Ansar, so giving up before the last hour disrespects the reward. He then warns, through the verse about the woman who unravels her own yarn, not to undo Ramadan's gains after Eid, since Shaytan returns to hunt for weaknesses. The second khutbah turns to Gaza's second Eid under bombing: Muslims are obligated to show joy and to pay zakat al-fitr locally so no child goes hungry, while giving to Gaza from the core of their wealth, not the surplus. He asks people to vote in the coming Canadian election on the single question of who supported genocide, and to keep London united on a single Eid by following the city's council of imams.

outline.heading: Opening
As long as a breath remains
outline.gist: Ramadan's counted days end as soon as you start counting them. Like a life with one breath left, in which sincere remorse can still bring acceptance, the month can be turned around with one moment left; the last ten nights were hidden so that we would keep working to the end.

outline.heading: Witness the last hour before Maghrib
outline.gist: He asks everyone to observe the final hour before sunset on the last day, when the gates of mercy close for another year, and to feel the month slipping through their fingers. Those moments may bring what the whole month did not.

outline.heading: The Prophet's tenth year and twenty-six refusals
outline.gist: After losing Khadijah and his uncle and three years of boycott, knowing he would have to leave Mecca, the Prophet spent the Hajj season going from tribe to tribe. Twenty-six attempts failed, some cruelly, and he was running out of days.

outline.heading: The last hour in Mina and six young men
outline.gist: He walked Mina until it was empty and, before leaving, saw six poor youths, the eldest 21, still waiting for someone to shave their heads. Because he gave it one last try, they returned with twelve, then seventy-two, and the ummah sitting here today is the result. Ramadan is not over either; quitting early disrespects the reward.

outline.heading: Make dua alone in the final hour
outline.gist: Close a door and make dua in the last hour of Ramadan. It will be the most heartfelt dua of your life, because you can feel the month leaving and know this Ramadan will never return.

outline.heading: Who was accepted? A farewell call
outline.gist: A Companion would stand in tears on the last night calling out to his people: who among us was accepted so we may congratulate him, and who was turned away so we may console him. Revise your intention, because tonight and all of tomorrow remain.

outline.heading: The fatigue fades, the reward stays
outline.gist: The tiredness of fasting disappears after a few hours of sleep and a few breakfasts, and you soon wonder how you did it, but the reward and the connection built this month stay with you.

outline.heading: Do not unravel the yarn
outline.gist: The Quranic proverb of the woman who unravels her firmly spun thread: do not ruin the closeness, ethics and spirituality built this month once it ends.

outline.heading: Shaytan returns with a vengeance
outline.gist: Set loose again, Shaytan knows exactly where to look for the walls you never built. Thirty days and nights destroyed eleven months of his work, so he and his helpers come back prepared; be ready for them.

outline.heading: Second khutbah: three quarters of a century
outline.gist: This is not a second bittersweet Eid but something closer to the seventy-sixth: for more than three quarters of a century the sacred lands have been occupied, and Muslims are targeted from China and Kashmir to Africa, Eastern Europe and South Asia.

outline.heading: Eid joy is still an obligation
outline.gist: Gaza faces a second Eid under bombs, mourning the dead and the missing. Even so, Allah obligates joy on Eid: smile, care for your family, delight your children, and pay zakat al-fitr so no child in your community wakes up hungry or without new clothes.

outline.heading: A joy that stays incomplete
outline.gist: We celebrate in obedience, but the joy will not be complete until the sacred lands return to their owners and the wrongs are righted, knowing other children are waking up without parents, limbs or homes.

outline.heading: Vote on one question: did you support genocide?
outline.gist: With a federal election coming, Muslims have the numbers to affect policy. Others will vote on the economy and healthcare; Muslims should ask one question and make those who ignored genocide pay for it at the polls. He cannot justify a Muslim community here that cannot do at least that.

outline.heading: Principle over the economy
outline.gist: Yes, the economy is the worst he has seen, but this is a matter of principle. Learn from Hikma, CMAC and NCCM, and even if, like him, you rarely vote and doubt it works, vote this time for the children killed over seventeen months.

outline.heading: A committee to empty Gaza; advocacy matters
outline.gist: Women and children are now killed in tents, and a government committee has been set up to displace Gazans into other countries. Protests, posts and money are not enough; advocacy has a real effect here, and he can no longer argue against it.

outline.heading: Zakat is local
outline.gist: Zakat stays in the city so that no child or family here feels left out on Eid; what goes to Gaza should not come from zakat.

outline.heading: Give Gaza from the core, not the surplus
outline.gist: To Gaza give from the core of your wealth and time, what you yourself need, never the extra. They are paying the tax for a sleeping, divided ummah that has to rediscover the unity the Prophet gave it.

outline.heading: One city, one Eid
outline.gist: Everyone in London should follow the city's council of imams; the day London has two Eids will be a sad day, and it is shameful that Canada does not begin and end its fast together. People confuse questions of legitimate scholarly difference, which should be left to the scholars, with uncompromisable values.

outline.heading: Outro

VtnyTHYFCMo.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 26: Sixth Night of Tahajjud
VtnyTHYFCMo.one_line: Reminders from the story of Yusuf: lives too busy to see clearly, night as the time to reconnect, and carrying Ramadan into the year.
VtnyTHYFCMo.summary: On the twenty-sixth night the reminders between the rakaat draw on the story of Yusuf. The speaker begins from the verse that Yusuf and his brothers hold signs for those who ask, saying the story carries lessons for every part of life, from politics and civic engagement to the way we treat our families. He then turns to the congregation: for most of the year our lives are so submerged in the race of work, school and the children's activities that we cannot see clearly. He links Yusuf's time in darkness to these nights, saying that moments of darkness are when a person can finally stop, think and reconnect with Allah, and he reminds them that the Prophet promised forgiveness of past sins to whoever stands in prayer in Ramadan with faith and hope of reward. He closes on Yusuf's words at the reunion, where he speaks of Shaytan having come between him and his brothers rather than blaming them. A second, shorter reminder later in the night asks how to carry what these nights restore into the rest of the year, so that ordinary life does not pull people away again.

8sMTmf6_yJk.title: Pointing Out the Obvious 5: Difficulties and Trials
8sMTmf6_yJk.one_line: Life is designed to contain hardship; the Muslim meets it with realistic expectations and a permanent state of striving (jihad), not pessimism or entitlement.
8sMTmf6_yJk.summary: The sheikh argues that something earlier Muslims took for granted has become unclear: life is built to contain difficulty, and entering it expecting otherwise guarantees misery. He defines fitna as a trial with the power to change a person, then sorts trials into those handed to you, those you bring on yourself (which carry a debt against the reward), those facing whole communities, and those of outcome, process or mindset, saying his own work targets mindset because it is the root. The healthy response is jihad understood as a permanent state of exerting effort, against problems and toward improvement, which turns every act, even rest, into worship; he regrets that the word became taboo after 9/11 and distinguishes it from combat. He then tackles the problem of pain: objecting to pain assumes one knows how to build a meaningful world without it, yet pain is what lets us define pleasure, grow and draw near to Allah, and patient endurance of unearned pain is pure reward. He closes on expectations: expect from Allah only what He promised, expect little from people and much from yourself, and treat realism as preparation rather than pessimism.

outline.heading: Why point out the obvious
outline.gist: Truths that were plain to the Companions have become blurred, so the series restates them as norms every Muslim should accept.

outline.heading: Life is promised to contain difficulty
outline.gist: Hardship is part of how nature was designed, and entering life expecting otherwise brings only disappointment; the objection itself betrays a sheltered upbringing.

outline.heading: Anything of value costs effort
outline.gist: Jannah and every real achievement require struggle; believing you are the exception is self-deception.

outline.heading: What fitna means in the Quran
outline.gist: Fitna is a trial carrying the potential to change your views, faith or relationships, not just any hardship.

outline.heading: Trials you are handed
outline.gist: Everyone, rich or poor, is dealt some hardship they did nothing to earn; recognising these is part of accepting qadar.

outline.heading: Trials you bring on yourself
outline.gist: Using a careful versus a reckless driver, he says both kinds earn reward for perseverance, but self-inflicted trials carry a debt of accountability while unearned ones are pure reward.

outline.heading: Trials facing communities and nations
outline.gist: Societies also face handed difficulties, like scarce resources, and self-made ones, like corruption.

outline.heading: Challenges of outcome: ethical, sexual, financial, social
outline.gist: Some problems are about what people do, such as harmful behaviours spreading in a community.

outline.heading: Challenges of process: the hospital triage example
outline.gist: Good ideas fail through poor execution; his quality-improvement work shows how bad process leaves patients unseen with no one accountable.

outline.heading: Challenges of mindset are the root
outline.gist: Poor understanding drives poor decisions and behaviour, which is why his teaching aims at mindset rather than patching outcomes.

outline.heading: National debt as a mindset problem
outline.gist: Economic band-aids fail because a consumerist mentality spends beyond its means and produces too little.

outline.heading: Realism is preparation, not pessimism
outline.gist: Knowing trials will come lets you use times of ease to strengthen yourself so hardship never blindsides you.

outline.heading: Jihad as a permanent state
outline.gist: The Muslim is always exerting effort, against a problem or toward an improvement; the opposite is a life of preserving effort and seeking permanent rest.

outline.heading: Comfort serves focused striving
outline.gist: Making life comfortable is fine when it frees attention for the striving you choose; retirees and elders can give their time fully to it.

outline.heading: Jihad as the peak of Islam
outline.gist: The word recurs throughout the Quran and the Prophet called it the top of the camel's hump; it completes a triangle with sabr and taqwa.

outline.heading: How the word became taboo after 9/11
outline.gist: Avoiding the word for two decades also lost its essence, which partly explains how poorly Muslims now understand trials.

outline.heading: Striving versus combat
outline.gist: Fighting was a later, specific permission, while striving was taught in Makkah before fighting was allowed.

outline.heading: The umbrella concept: every act becomes worship
outline.gist: When life itself is striving for Allah, food, work and even rest that restores you fall under that goal and are rewarded.

outline.heading: Life will not let you live carefree
outline.gist: Those who chase permanent leisure are eventually dealt a hard hand, like an unexplained cancer, and are crushed if their mindset was wrong; desert life once forced the right mindset.

outline.heading: Surat al-Ankabut: no one is left untested
outline.gist: Allah tests every claimant of faith so their actions expose whether the claim is true.

outline.heading: The problem of pain is a silly question
outline.gist: Asking why God allowed pain assumes one knows how to create a meaningful living universe without it.

outline.heading: Reflect on pain instead of fight or flight
outline.gist: Pain marks life and drives growth; quoting Ray Dalio, he urges reflecting at the moment of pain when clarity is greatest.

outline.heading: Things are known through their opposites
outline.gist: Without pain, ease, joy and pleasure cannot be defined, like sugar to someone who never tasted salt.

outline.heading: The congenitally blind brain
outline.gist: People given sight late cannot interpret it because the brain never had a contrast, showing that understanding depends on comparison.

outline.heading: The paradox of suffering
outline.gist: Those who suffer most often turn to God; suffering teaches gratitude, and over-protected children grow entitled and immature.

outline.heading: His teacher dismisses a marital complaint
outline.gist: An elderly sheikh sent away a student complaining about his righteous wife, showing how suffering clarifies priorities.

outline.heading: The prophets are tested most
outline.gist: Trials increase with closeness to Allah, so more tests mean more chances to rise.

outline.heading: Unearned hardship is tax-free reward
outline.gist: Patiently endured trials are what you will hope to find in your record; it is the moments of ease you will worry about.

outline.heading: Even a thorn removes sins
outline.gist: The hadith on every discomfort expiating sins assumes a believer who is already striving and patient.

outline.heading: Pain as a reason to reject God after the Arab Spring
outline.gist: Mass torture and displacement made suffering a leading cause of lost faith; our duty is to relieve pain and we are accountable when we do not.

outline.heading: Every pain is temporary
outline.gist: Countless things could go wrong at any moment; what remains after pain is the perseverance shown.

outline.heading: Pain drives all growth
outline.gist: From the first cell onward, life moves to escape pain; the Muslim also accepts that some pain cannot be dodged and strives through it.

outline.heading: Islam is designed to alleviate pain
outline.gist: Its rulings on health, zakat, prayer and social life remove physical, financial, mental and social pain; abandoning them adds needless suffering.

outline.heading: Expectations govern happiness
outline.gist: Expect trials in marriage, parenting and work; expecting much from others and little from yourself makes you miserable.

outline.heading: What you may expect from Allah
outline.gist: Only what He promised: justice, trials and reward for doing your part; demanding more is entitlement, since we already live in His debt.

outline.heading: Expecting ease from the world is ignorance
outline.gist: The world owes you nothing and will not make you happy.

outline.heading: The clinic example
outline.gist: The same number of patients feels like a bad or good day depending only on what he expected.

outline.heading: Realism versus pessimism
outline.gist: Pessimism refuses to accept ease when it comes; realism expects difficulty and turns that into a mindset of striving.

outline.heading: Expectations in marriage
outline.gist: Expect more from yourself and less from your spouse; two people waiting on each other cannot be resolved.

outline.heading: Expect little from people, more from those you raise
outline.gist: He expects nothing from people generally, but must expect more of students and children, which costs him frustration.

outline.heading: The Prophet held the committed to a higher standard
outline.gist: He excused the hypocrites but boycotted Ka'b ibn Malik for fifty days because more was expected of a true believer.

ONSTpa3EVdI.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 26: Maintaining the Balance
ONSTpa3EVdI.one_line: Balance as a Quranic theme: the mizan of creation, the Book and iron sent together, and knowing priorities when loyalties conflict.
ONSTpa3EVdI.summary: He presents balance as a theme that runs through every part of life, not only religion. Climate change and overconsumption show what happens when humans tip a finely balanced system. In Ar-Rahman 55:7-9 the word mizan appears four times; he explains that it means balance before it means scale, that creation exists because of that balance, and that human freedom can either ruin or protect it. Imbalance is not inequality of reward but rigged scales where some starve while others consume without limit, and history shows such imbalance corrects itself violently. In Al-Hadid 57:25 the prophets were sent with clear proofs, the Book and the Balance, plus iron: every act of worship needs both its outer form and its inner intention, and anything sacred must be protected, since a book without strength is trampled and strength without guidance becomes brutality, as seen in the killing of children in Gaza. In Al-Mujadilah 58:22, revealed when companions faced relatives at Badr, balance means knowing priorities: Allah's command outranks even love of parents. He urges the community to prioritize advocacy, outreach, pooled finances, education and mentorship over buildings, and to stop dividing over disputed fiqh.

outline.heading: Climate change as a broken balance
outline.gist: Global warming, coal burning and overconsumption tip a balanced system; the poor pay the price and humans, not the planet, will suffer.

outline.heading: A middle nation that knows how far to go
outline.gist: Balance runs through the whole Quran; the ummah is praised as wasat, balanced rather than mediocre.

outline.heading: Mizan means balance before scale
outline.gist: The word is repeated four times; a scale is called mizan only because it is used to reach balance, as on the market scales of his childhood.

outline.heading: Answering the refrain of Ar-Rahman
outline.gist: The surah counts Allah's blessings; the listener should answer each 'which of the favours' by affirming he denies none of them.

outline.heading: Creation exists because of the balance
outline.gist: Allah set the laws that govern the universe, and humanity is a product of that balance.

outline.heading: Free will can ruin or protect the balance
outline.gist: Choice and intellect let humans either tilt the scales or maintain and improve them; Allah commands not to transgress.

outline.heading: Enough for need, not for greed
outline.gist: All living things have a right to exist; the earth has enough for everyone's needs but not for everyone's greed.

outline.heading: Establish weighing with justice
outline.gist: Do not take more for yourself and less for others when dealing within the balance.

outline.heading: Cheating the scales today
outline.gist: Like those who take full measure and give short, people now consume resources far beyond their portion.

outline.heading: Balance, not equality, and how imbalance corrects itself
outline.gist: Working harder may earn more, but some starving while others overindulge is imbalance, and history shows it is corrected harshly.

outline.heading: Rigged scales lead to chaos
outline.gist: Prophetic teachings about the end times point to oppression that breeds killing and anarchy once people have been deprived too long.

outline.heading: A word repeated four times demands reflection
outline.gist: Repetition signals emphasis: balance is needed in religion, ethics, finance and society, with no one above the law.

outline.heading: Al-Hadid: balancing two things instead of choosing one
outline.gist: After a cluster of surahs presenting choices, Al-Hadid asks for balance between the spiritual and the physical.

outline.heading: Messengers sent with proofs, the Book and the Balance
outline.gist: The prophets brought clear ethical guidance, a book teaching who we are, and a balanced approach to life.

outline.heading: Neither the body over the spirit nor the reverse
outline.gist: The balance means not indulging the physical while neglecting the spirit, nor obsessing over the spiritual while ignoring the physical.

outline.heading: Every prophet taught the same balance
outline.gist: Other traditions drifted to one side and walk with a limp; the Quran keeps both.

outline.heading: Outer form and inner intention in worship
outline.gist: Prayer needs wudu and the intent to worship Allah; hajj has rites and meaning; no deed is accepted without both.

outline.heading: And We sent down iron
outline.gist: Iron brings strength and benefit: weapons, shields, buildings and civilization to defend the way of life.

outline.heading: Something sacred must be protected
outline.gist: A beautiful way of life that no one is willing to defend will be trampled by those who invested in strength.

outline.heading: Iron without the Book, the Book without iron
outline.gist: Strength without guidance murders children on live television; guidance without strength is never heard. Allah tests who holds both.

outline.heading: The ummah trying to pick up both again
outline.gist: Muslims dropped both for a time; lifting them again is heavy, and he hopes the next generation succeeds.

outline.heading: Context of Al-Mujadilah: facing a father at Badr
outline.gist: A companion found his father in the opposing army and did not know whether to stand with the Prophet.

outline.heading: No allegiance to those fighting Allah, even kin
outline.gist: In the battlefield context, believers do not side with those trying to destroy the faith, even parents, children or tribe.

outline.heading: Balance includes knowing what comes first
outline.gist: Loving parents is commanded, but nothing equals Allah's commands; a distorted priority list ruins the balance.

outline.heading: Priorities in every system: emergency room triage
outline.gist: Health, law, politics and education all run on priorities; in the ER, life and limb come before abdominal pain.

outline.heading: A Medinan verse balancing three Meccan verses
outline.gist: After honouring parents was established in Mecca, this verse clarified that it does not apply when the deen itself is under attack, which relieved the companions.

outline.heading: The community's misplaced priorities
outline.gist: He repeats that advocacy, outreach, financial centralization, education and mentorship matter more than structures and spaces.

outline.heading: Stop dividing over disputed fiqh
outline.gist: Questions scholars have long differed on, such as how Eid is determined, do not deserve hours of argument that split communities.

outline.heading: Outro

GGZ4CCEp_ok.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 17: Envy and Anger
GGZ4CCEp_ok.one_line: Envy and anger as the two toxic results of self-value swinging low, with their Quranic examples and practical cures.
GGZ4CCEp_ok.summary: Continuing his image of self-value as a pendulum, he examines what happens when it swings toward inferiority. Envy is discomfort at someone else having something, not a wish to have it yourself; healthy aspiration is a different thing and the Prophet allowed it only for knowledge and generous wealth. Envy comes from attaching value to things and seeing others as threats. He ranks three kinds: envy over worldly goods, envy over worldly gains reached through religious work, and the subtlest, envy over someone's closeness to Allah, which is what drove Qabil. Both Quranic envy stories, Qabil and Habil and Yusuf's brothers, involve siblings and murder, and he corrects the popular marriage explanation of the first. The cure is a jama'ah mindset: seeing everyone as teammates so their success is your win, asking yourself repeatedly why you felt discomfort, and becoming the person people want to share good news with, while being careful not to provoke envy in others. Anger arises when self-value is threatened; every emotion born of fluctuating self-value is toxic, unlike anger for Allah's sake at oppression. Whoever can trigger you holds your remote control. Through children who sense ego-driven anger and a road-rage example, he shows that envy and anger are about us, and asks people to find their triggers and respond calmly.

outline.heading: The pendulum of self-value swinging low
outline.gist: Self-value granted by Allah should never fluctuate; when it swings up we get vanity and arrogance, and this session looks at what happens when it swings down.

outline.heading: Hasad defined: not wanting others to have it
outline.gist: Envy is a heaviness at seeing others do well; it is not wanting what they have but not wanting them to have it, and it can be very subtle.

outline.heading: Envy grows from assigning value to things
outline.gist: When we attach worth to status or attention, someone else gaining it feels like a threat to the nafs, even though there is enough for everyone.

outline.heading: Ghibtah: healthy aspiration
outline.gist: Being inspired to achieve what another has is not envy; the Prophet considered it worthwhile only for knowledge used well and wealth spent for Allah.

outline.heading: Notice even a second of discomfort
outline.gist: When you hear of someone's success and feel a flicker of unease, ask yourself why rather than brushing it off.

outline.heading: Qabil and Habil's offerings
outline.gist: Habil offered his best sheep and Qabil his worst crops; Allah accepted Habil's, and Qabil's envy was over acceptance by Allah.

outline.heading: First type of envy: over worldly things
outline.gist: Envy over someone's wealth or house is so petty that scholars of tazkiyah refuse to discuss it; it shows a deep distortion of one's view of reality.

outline.heading: Second type: worldly gain earned through deen
outline.gist: The most common envy is over the admiration or status someone gets from religious work, such as a Quran memorizer; be inspired to do the same instead.

outline.heading: Third type: envy over closeness to Allah
outline.gist: The subtlest and most dangerous envy is being bothered that someone is drawing nearer to Allah or giving more, even unseen.

outline.heading: Qabil's raw threat and Habil's answer
outline.gist: Qabil blurted out that he would kill his brother; Habil told him Allah accepts from the mindful, but Qabil cared only that his brother was accepted.

outline.heading: Seeking refuge from the envier in Al-Falaq
outline.gist: The surah ends with refuge from the envier because one dot of envy in the heart can grow into something enormous.

outline.heading: The Quran makes it about acceptance, not marriage
outline.gist: The popular story of a disputed bride is not in the Quran; the issue was whose attention we crave, people's or Allah's.

outline.heading: Yusuf's brothers and their father's attention
outline.gist: They envied the attention Yusuf got from Yaqub and planned to kill him or throw him in a well; both envy stories involve siblings and murder.

outline.heading: Reflect on your own small envies
outline.gist: Recall moments when another's achievement caused you slight discomfort and ask why.

outline.heading: The cure: a jama'ah team mentality
outline.gist: We wear the same jersey with different numbers; a good teammate wants players better than himself, and this view should extend to family, community and all humanity.

outline.heading: First tool: ask yourself why, several times
outline.gist: Identify what you attached value to, whether job, popularity or position, that someone else's success seemed to threaten.

outline.heading: Second tool: be the one they want to tell
outline.gist: Rejoice genuinely in others' good news and support them; people sense sincerity and will come to you first.

outline.heading: Comparison breeds depression and anxiety
outline.gist: A person alone on an island may be hungry and lonely but not depressed or anxious, because there is no one to compare with.

outline.heading: Do not generate envy in others
outline.gist: Share successes with those who love you and failures with those who truly love you; envy has an unseen power, and showing off can also breed arrogance.

outline.heading: Anger as a response to threatened self-value
outline.gist: When someone makes you feel less, the nafs tries to swing the pendulum back through anger.

outline.heading: Every emotion from fluctuating self-value is toxic
outline.gist: Vanity, arrogance, envy, anger and even love born of fluctuating worth are toxic; genuine emotions exist only when self-value is stable.

outline.heading: Losing status and the advice not to act in anger
outline.gist: People who draw worth from their image lose their temper when lowered before others; the Prophet warned against speaking or deciding while angry.

outline.heading: Anger for the sake of Allah is different
outline.gist: Anger at oppression, harm or disrespect of Allah's commands is not tied to self-value, so it stays under control.

outline.heading: Whoever triggers you holds your remote control
outline.gist: If someone knows your button, they control your behaviour even if you beat them; that makes you weak, not strong.

outline.heading: Children feel the difference in a parent's anger
outline.gist: Kids sense whether you discipline them for their good or lash out because they threaten your image or authority as a parent.

outline.heading: Road rage and the story we tell ourselves
outline.gist: Learning the other driver's wife is in labour erases the anger, showing that it came from our assumptions and self-value, not from them.

outline.heading: Self-value and mortality as the foundations
outline.gist: Without clarity on self-value and mortality, most diseases of the heart persist; with them, the Quran teaches the rest.

outline.heading: The Prophet's remedy for anger
outline.gist: Shaytan blows on the spark of anger; calm yourself, make wudu, step away and return to speak once calm.

outline.heading: The calm response is the strong one
outline.gist: You can still put someone in their place, but doing it composed shows strength while the angry response shows vulnerability.
